doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

chapter: Dixieland and the college jazz scene
title: Black and white musicians in record collections; Dixieland's popularity
summary: Collier says young fans did not notice race and listened to mixed collections; he insists Dixieland, not swing, was most popular into the mid-fifties.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there a distinction with you guys in your listening between black and white bands or black and white artists?

Nobody even knew. Nobody cared. The black and white thing didn’t exist. It did not exist. You were — you know Johnny Hodges would be, you know everybody’s favorite alto player. Nobody ever heard of a baritone sax player better than Harry Carney. Louis of course. But you would listen to Louis and you would turn around and listen to Beiderbecke who was white. You would listen to Jack Teagarden and you’d turn around and listen to Dickie Wells who was black. You’d listen to the great black saxophone player, Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young, all these guys. There was no problem. If you looked at a typical collection of records from somebody from those days they’d be completely mixed. Completely mixed. Billy Banks Rhythm Makers, that was a mixed band. They had black and white guys in it. It was a recording band only, but it was mixed. You didn’t know the difference.
How many people in your fraternity had record players?

Well I think a lot of them did. A lot of them did. And then there was a big fancy record player in the living room. So before lunch we’d all be down there playing Hot Fives or something or other, Pee Wee Russell, who knows, arguing about who was better. You had all of Pee Wee Russell. Typical stuff. But you see this, if you read the histories, you go right from the swing bands, where they say this is the only time jazz was popular in the United States, most of that wasn’t jazz. That’s completely wrong. You go right from there to bebop, to Bird and — but the main thing during those years from say the very late thirties through most of the fifties, say until ’55 or somewhere up in there, was this Dixieland jazz was the most popular.
